title: The Red Kite
text: On Saturday morning, Ben and his dad went to the park. Ben took his new red kite. The wind was strong, so the kite went up very fast. Ben let out more string. The kite flew higher and higher until it was a tiny red dot in the sky. Then the wind suddenly stopped. The kite began to fall. Ben ran across the grass, pulling the string as fast as he could. Just before the kite landed in the pond, the wind came back. Ben's dad laughed out loud. "That was close!" he said. Ben held on tight and smiled.

title: Hedgehogs
text: Hedgehogs are small animals with sharp spines on their backs. They often live in gardens, parks and woods. Hedgehogs sleep during the day and come out at night to look for food. They eat beetles, worms, slugs and snails. When a hedgehog is scared, it rolls into a tight ball so its spines stick out all around it. In winter, hedgehogs find a quiet, safe place and sleep for many long months. This is called hibernation. Their bodies use very little energy while they sleep, so they can stay alive until spring comes and there is food to eat again.

title: The Swimming Club
text: Kai was nervous. It was his first day at the swimming club, and he did not know anyone there. He stood at the edge of the pool and looked at the deep water. "Come on in," called a girl with a blue hat. "I'm Priya. The water is not as cold as it looks." Kai took a deep breath and stepped down the ladder. The water was cool but not freezing. Soon he was kicking his legs and laughing. By the end of the lesson, he had learned to float on his back and had made a brand new friend.

title: Market Day
text: Every Sunday, the town square is turned into a busy market. Stalls line the cobbled streets, covered with striped canvas roofs in red, yellow and green. The air smells of fresh bread, roasting nuts and sticky honey. Farmers shout out their prices, hoping to attract customers to their crates of shiny apples and juicy tomatoes. A man with a violin plays lively tunes near the fountain while children weave between the crowds. By midday, the square is so full of shoppers that it is hard to walk in a straight line. It is a lovely place to spend a morning.

title: Fishing at Dawn
text: Yasmin's grandfather had promised to teach her how to fish. They rose before dawn and carried their rods down to the quiet lake. Mist floated over the water like a soft, grey blanket. "The secret is patience," whispered Grandad, passing Yasmin a wriggling worm. Yasmin threaded it onto the hook and cast her line. Minutes slowly ticked by. Nothing happened. Yasmin was beginning to feel bored when the float suddenly bobbed under the surface. She gripped her rod tightly and reeled as fast as she could. At the end of her line, a silver fish flashed in the morning sunlight.

title: How Volcanoes Erupt
text: Volcanoes form where hot, melted rock called magma pushes up from deep beneath the Earth's surface. As the magma rises, pressure builds up inside the mountain, much like the fizz in a shaken bottle of lemonade. Eventually, the pressure becomes far too great and the volcano erupts. Molten rock, ash and gases burst out of an opening at the top of the mountain. Once the magma flows out of the volcano, it is known as lava. The lava cools and hardens into solid rock. Over many years, repeated eruptions build up layers, making the volcano taller and wider over time.

title: The Talent Show
text: Zara had been dreading the school talent show all week. Her friends had signed up to dance and juggle, but she could only play the recorder, and not very well. As she waited behind the curtain, her palms felt clammy and her stomach churned wildly. "You'll be fine," whispered her teacher. Zara walked onto the stage and lifted the recorder to her lips. The first note wobbled, but she kept going. Slowly, the tune grew steadier. When she finished, the audience erupted into applause. Zara grinned so widely that her cheeks ached, and she wondered why she had ever worried.

title: Why We Should Recycle
text: Recycling is one of the simplest ways we can look after our planet. When we throw away paper, plastic and glass, they often end up buried in enormous landfill sites, where they can take hundreds of years to break down. However, if we sort these materials into separate bins, they can be collected and turned into useful new products. Recycling aluminium cans uses far less energy than making brand-new ones. It also means that fewer trees are cut down and less pollution is released into the air. Everyone, young or old, can make a real difference by recycling every day.

title: The Old Lighthouse
text: The old lighthouse had been empty for years, but Josh was convinced he could see a light flickering in the top window. Late one evening, he crept along the cliff path with a small torch, his heart thumping loudly. The wooden door creaked as he pushed it open. Inside, thick cobwebs hung from the ceiling like ragged curtains. He climbed the spiral staircase, one step at a time, until he reached the lamp room. There, sitting calmly on a wooden crate with a candle beside her, was a girl reading a book. "Shh," she said quietly. "You'll scare the seagulls."

title: Life in a Hive
text: Honeybees live together in enormous colonies, sometimes containing tens of thousands of individuals. Each bee has a job. The queen lays all the eggs, worker bees gather nectar and pollen from flowers, and drones mate with the queen. When a worker discovers a good source of nectar, she returns to the hive and performs a special "waggle dance". The direction and length of the dance tell the other bees exactly where to find the flowers. Without bees, many of the fruits and vegetables we enjoy would not grow, because bees carry pollen from one plant to another as they feed.

title: The Letter
text: Eleanor gazed at the letter in her trembling hands, unsure whether to laugh or cry. For months, she had rehearsed what she would say if she ever won the scholarship, yet now all her carefully chosen words had completely vanished. Her father watched silently from the doorway, hardly daring to breathe. "Well?" he asked eventually. "Don't keep me in suspense." Eleanor looked up, her eyes shining. "I got it," she whispered, and then, louder, "I actually got it!" Her father rushed across the room and swept her into a hug so tight that the letter fluttered gently to the floor.

title: Phones for Children?
text: Some people argue that children should not be given mobile phones until they are at least twelve years old. They claim that phones distract pupils from schoolwork and encourage them to spend far too much time indoors. Furthermore, young children may come across websites that are unsuitable for their age. On the other hand, supporters point out that phones allow parents to contact their children in an emergency. They also say that learning to use technology responsibly is a valuable skill. Perhaps the best solution is for families to agree on sensible rules together, balancing the benefits against the risks.

title: The Odd Socks
text: Tentatively, Amira pushed open the heavy classroom door, expecting a reprimand for being late. Instead, the room fell silent. Twenty-eight faces swivelled towards her, and Mr Okafor put down his red marker pen with deliberate slowness. "Amira," he said, "would you care to explain why you are wearing one green sock and one orange one?" She glanced down in dismay. In her frantic rush that morning, she had failed to notice the mismatch. A ripple of giggles spread across the room. Amira felt her ears burning, yet somehow she found herself smiling. "It's a new fashion trend," she announced proudly.

title: Why the Tide Turns
text: Twice a day, the sea rises up the shore and then slowly drains away again. These movements are called tides, and they are caused mainly by the Moon. The Moon’s gravity pulls on the Earth, and because water can move freely, the oceans bulge towards it. As the Earth spins, different coastlines pass through the bulge, so the water level rises and falls. Fishermen, sailors and beachcombers all depend on tide tables to predict when the water will be at its highest. Ignoring them can be dangerous, since a rising tide can cut off a beach within a few minutes.

title: The Violin
text: Ruby’s heart hammered as the auctioneer raised his wooden gavel. For weeks, she had admired the battered old violin in the dusty shop window, imagining the music it might make. Now, with only twelve pounds in her coat pocket, she watched the bidding climb steadily beyond her reach. A hush settled over the crowded room. Then, from the back, an elderly man’s voice rang out: “Sold, to the young lady in the green coat!” Ruby spun round in sheer astonishment. The man winked kindly, pressed the violin into her trembling hands and murmured, “Somebody once did the same for me.”

title: Should Zoos Exist?
text: Zoos have long divided public opinion. Supporters argue that they protect endangered species by breeding rare animals that might otherwise vanish forever. They say that visiting a zoo helps young people to care about wildlife. Critics disagree. They believe that wild animals should not live in enclosures, however large, and they point out that many captive animals pace up and down, which suggests they are unhappy. Very few zoo-bred animals are ever returned to the wild, so critics ask whether zoos really help. In the end, each person must weigh the benefits against the concerns and decide where they stand.

title: The Storm
text: By the time the storm reached the headland, Elsa had already secured every rattling shutter. Wind screamed around the lantern room, and the ancient stone tower shuddered as waves pounded the rocks below. She tightened her grip on the rail, gazing out at the churning darkness. Somewhere out there, beyond the reef, a ship was struggling. Without hesitation, she relit the great brass lamp, its beam slicing through the driving rain. For hours she stayed grimly at her post, weary but unyielding, until at first light a small fishing boat limped safely into the harbour, its exhausted crew waving gratefully.

title: The Envelope
text: The letter arrived on the coldest morning of the whole year, wedged between an unpaid gas bill and a takeaway menu. Nora recognised the spidery handwriting at once, and her stomach tightened. For three years, her grandfather’s silence had hung over the family like a stubborn fog, and nobody would explain why. She slid a trembling finger beneath the flap, hesitating. What if the words inside only made everything worse? Then, before she could change her mind, she tore the envelope open and began to read, her breath clouding the frosty window as the house creaked and settled around her.

title: The Rosetta Stone
text: In 1799, French soldiers repairing an old fort in Egypt uncovered a slab of dark grey stone covered in strange writing. The Rosetta Stone, as it became known, carried the same message in three different scripts: hieroglyphs, a simpler Egyptian script and ancient Greek. Scholars could easily read Greek, so they compared the three versions line by line. Even so, it took more than twenty years for a French linguist, Jean-François Champollion, to work out how hieroglyphs worked. His discovery, announced in 1822, allowed people to read thousands of years of Egyptian history for the first time in many centuries.
